discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: A front will move over Western Washington today. The front will lift north tonight ending up in British Columbia Wednesday. A cold front will stall offshore Wednesday into Thursday. What is left of the front moving through Thursday night. Additional weather systems will move through Friday through Sunday. An upper level trough will move over the area Sunday night and Monday.
hydrology: A flood watch has been issued for Mason county for the possibility of the Skokomish River flooding with this next round of rain. The buffer from the dry October is gone with the river only dropping to around a foot and a half below flood stage after this recent rain event. As mentioned earlier this is a juicy system moving into the area today. Model 850 mb winds 40 to 50 knots out of the southwest creating good orographics over the south slopes of the Olympics. Snow levels will also be high, around 9000 feet. Forecasted rain amounts for the 24 hours between 4 AM today and 4 AM Wednesday along the south slopes 2.5 to 4 inches. With the elevated snow levels and the river running high already there is a good chance the Skokomish river will reach flood stage this evening or in the early morning hours Wednesday. Another round of rainfall with the system Friday could also push the Skokomish back above flood stage.
River flooding not expected on the other rivers in the area in the next 7 days. Felton

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A front will move over Western Washington today. The front will lift north tonight ending up in British Columbia Wednesday. A cold front will stall offshore Wednesday into Thursday. What is left of the front moving through Thursday night. Additional weather systems will move through Friday through Sunday. An upper level trough will move over the area Sunday night and Monday.

sections.title: Short term (today through Thursday)
paragraphs: Several headlines are already in place to cover this round of weather impacts. Will look further into possible minor coastal flooding in San Juan and western Whatcom county around the time of high tide Wednesday morning. 33

Previous discussion...Satellite imagery shows cloudy skies over Western Washington early this morning. Doppler radar has rain out ahead of the next system reached the coast around 3 AM/11Z. Temperatures were in the mid 40s to lower 50s.

Juicy system moving into Western Washington today. IVT values in the 800-1000 kg/m/s range making for a rainy day across the area. Southwesterly winds aloft will create the usual rain shadow northeast of the Olympics but with the air mass so moist even that area will fill in with rain later today. In addition to the rain, winds will be increasing later this morning into the afternoon hours. Model 925 mb winds 40-50 knots along the coast and just slightly weaker over the Northwest Interior beginning around 21Z. These winds will mix down towards the surface at times. The wind advisory for the coastal beaches and Northwest Interior beginning at 1 PM will remain in effect for gusts as high as 50 mph. The combination of winds, waves and lower surface pressure around the time of high tides will produce some minor coastal flooding along the ocean beaches. Inundation of 1.5 to 2 feet above ground levels is possible between 10 AM and 3 PM. Highs today in the mid 50s to lower 60s.

Front hanging over Western Washington this evening before lifting north overnight with rain chances becoming confined to west of Puget Sound and the Northwest Interior by early Wednesday morning. Front still close enough to keep windy conditions going along the coast and in the Northwest Interior. With the cloud cover and southerly winds it is going to be a mild night with lows in the lower to mid 50s. Record high minimums are possible.

Little change in the pattern Wednesday with the front to the north and a cold front stalled offshore. Rain along the coast and over the Olympics continuing with cloudy skies over most of the remainder of the area. Breezy southerly winds continuing throughout the day warming daytime temperatures into the 60s. Record highs are also possible.

Cold front remaining stalled offshore Wednesday night but not far enough off the coast to keep rain away for the coastline. Winds easing Wednesday evening with surface gradients relaxing and winds aloft decreasing. Plenty of cloud cover over the area making for another mild night with lows near 50.

Stalled cold front becoming more north south oriented Thursday as an upper level trough behind the front digs south offshore. Front will still be close enough to give locations west of Puget Sound more rain. Mild temperatures continuing with highs in the upper 50s to mid 60s. Felton

sections.title: Long term (Thursday night through Monday)
paragraphs: Models in good agreement with the stalled front getting kicked inland Thursday night as the flow aloft consolidates over the Eastern Pacific. Earlier model solutions indicated more of an atmospheric river pattern with the river getting stuck over the area Friday and Saturday. Model solutions are still wet for the Friday through the weekend but instead of an atmospheric river the solutions now favor a pair of wet and windy frontal systems Friday and again Saturday night and Sunday. Upper level trough trailing the front for Sunday night and Monday. Snow levels remaining above pass levels until the upper level trough arrives Sunday night lowering the snow level down to the 3500 to 4000 foot range. Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Ceilings will continue to fill in and lower this morning as the next system moves in and brings the next round of rain which will persist through much of the day today. MVFR conditions across much of the interior in showers. Some periods of localized IFR conditions cannot be ruled out. Ceilings look to gradually improve to low- end VFR from south to north this evening for the interior terminals as the rain begins to lift north and taper off. MVFR conditions look to remain along the coast. South/southeasterly winds will build this morning to around 10-15 kt and remain fairly steady through the period. Gusts up to 20-25 kt will be possible area- wide, with gusts increasing up to 35 kt along the coast and north interior locations tonight.

KSEA...VFR to MVFR conditions early this morning as rain moves through the terminal. Low chances for IFR conditions (around 20%) through 21z. Ceilings look to gradually raise this evening as rain tapers off, with VFR conditions expected after around 03Z tonight. Winds remain S/SE 8- 12kt with gusts up to 20 kt possible at times this afternoon and into tonight.
62/Mazurkiewicz

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds will continue to increase over the area waters through this morning and afternoon, peaking this evening and persisting through the overnight hours tonight into early Wednesday. Winds will reach up to gale force across the coastal waters and the East Strait of Juan de Fuca, with Small Craft Advisories from Admiralty Inlet through the Northern Inland Waters as well. Winds will start to very slowly ease throughout the day Wednesday, with winds finally easing below advisory thresholds area-wide by Wednesday evening as the stalled front offshore causing these winds falls apart.

Seas around 9 to 10 ft will rise this morning to 16 to 19 ft this afternoon and evening both due to the stronger winds and another westerly swell group arriving. Seas will remain high through Wednesday morning before slowly easing throughout the day Thursday, through remaining above 11-13 ft.

The next stronger low pressure system begins to move into the coastal waters and increase the area winds late Thursday night into Friday. Winds look to peak Friday morning, with guidance still showing 60-75% chances for storm force wind gusts over the coastal waters. Winds look to ease slightly Friday night before another wave brings another round of strong winds on Saturday (40-55% chc of storm force gusts) and into Saturday night. Winds look to finally ease below thresholds late Sunday as the low broadens and weakens as it moves onshore.

Guidance has shifted the largest waves slightly farther south towards southern Washington and Oregon, but remains very confident (60-80%) in seas building above 20 ft on Friday, with GEFS and ECMWF probabilities showing 25-35% chances of seas above 25 ft. Slight shifts in the low tracks will determine where the dynamic fetch effects will be maximized from these systems, with seas nearing or exceeding 30 ft still not out of the equation, especially towards the southern portions of the waters.

sections.title: Morning update
paragraphs: A Flood Advisory has been issued for the Portland/Vancouver Metro Area through 2 PM this afternoon due to heavy rain which is leading to minor flooding in low-lying and poor drainage areas. Ponding of water on roads is occurring. Around 0.40- 0.80" of rain has fallen in the last 12 hours, and 0.25-0.40" in the last hour. Be aware of your surroundings and do not drive on flooded roads. Rain is expected to decrease this afternoon.  -10

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Monday...Water vapor satellite imagery early Tuesday morning depicts a large swatch of moisture approaching the northern PacNW. This is the next atmospheric river slated to impact the region as the associated frontal system will slowly approach the WA and far northern OR coast today through Wednesday. Some light scattered showers are possible early this morning across all of NW OR and SW WA before upper level ridging begins building east of the Cascades, limiting the main bulk of the precipitation to locations north of US-20 this morning then steadily moving north into Washington through the afternoon.  A rather sharp gradient in rainfall totals on Tuesday is expected from south to north, with little to no rain south of US-20, less than 0.2 inch for the interior lowlands south of Longview and the coast south of Tillamook, 0.25-0.5 inches for the SW WA Cascades and the coast from Tillamook to the state line, and 0.5-1 inch for Pacific County. Heavier rain associated with this atmospheric river is expected over the Olympic Peninsula. Expect another round of breezy southerly winds with gusts as high as 30-40 mph along the coast north of Tillamook and SW WA west of I-5 through this evening.

Upper-level ridging will reach its peak amplitude on Wednesday, supporting dry and unseasonably warm temperatures across interior valleys with high temperatures forecast in the low to mid 60s. Daily record high temperatures look to remain out of reach for most locations, though the record values of 64F at Portland (PDX) and Hillsboro (HIO) set in 1989 and 66F at Vancouver (VUO) set in 1904, 1907, and 1930 may be in jeopardy. However, showers will continue in Pacific County and along the coast north of Tillamook. Thursday is expected to be a transition day as upper ridging begins shifting east as upper troughing begins pushing into the northeastern Pacific. Daytime temperatures will lower a few degrees, though will still be unseasonably warm in the low 60s across interior valleys. Mostly dry weather is expected through the day except for a 20-40% chance of showers along the coast, mainly due to uncertainty on specific timing of the rain from the next approaching trough.

There is high confidence that an upper-level low pressure system will become situated over the northeast Pacific west of Canada from late Thursday/Friday into the weekend, returning troughing to the Pacific Northwest. Multiple surface frontal systems are expected to move through the region during this time, bringing repeated chances for widespread rain and breezy winds. There is still uncertainty with specific rainfall amounts and peak wind gusts; however, we can say for certain that it will be wet. This is shaping up to be another atmospheric river event as long-range ensembles indicate a 70-90% chance for vapor transport to exceed 500 kg/(ms) at the leading edge of this trough on Friday somewhere along the Oregon coast with similar probabilities of vapor transport values remaining above 250 kg/(ms) into Sunday. Increasingly saturated soils from multiple weather systems could allow for greater runoff into area rivers, meaning at least isolated flooding cannot be ruled out. People should also clear gutters and storm drains of any leaves or debris to prevent urban flooding. Across the Cascades, it appears that this system will be warm enough to keep snow levels between 5500-6500 feet, keeping the passes snow-free. However, Cascade peaks could see a few inches of snow combined between Friday night and Saturday night, with even more over the volcanoes.

When it comes to winds, there is a 20-40% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 55 mph along the coast Friday and Saturday, with the highest chances on Friday. Wind gusts of this magnitude could result in scattered or widespread power outages or tree damage. Along the I- 5 corridor, there is a 15-30% chance for maximum wind gusts exceeding 40 mph, which could result in isolated power outages or tree damage. To prepare, make sure to secure loose outdoor items. -03/10

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 18Z Wednesday...A slow moving frontal band remains draped across Northwest OR and southwest WA, bringing persistent light to moderate rain to the region. Conditions vary across the are but most terminals are MVFR or IFR as rain impacts the terminals. Conditions are expected to improve for many terminals except KAST as the front shifts northward. Inland winds from the south 7-10 kts. Gusty southerly winds along the coast with gusts up to 25-30 kts.
Cloud cover overnight could thin enough to allow for some patchy fog but chances are low at 10-20%, mainly in the coast range. Will continue to monitor conditions for possible changes.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Moderate to light rain continues as a frontal band sits over the region. Expecting this to shift northward early this afternoon but will continue to support MVFR or lower conditions for a couple more hours. Conditions trend toward VFR this afternoon. Winds southerly around 5-7 kt, shifting southeasterly this afternoon at less than 5 kt. -19

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Small craft conditions continue across the waters this morning in the wake of a frontal system. Winds will increase this morning across the waters and remain elevated through Wednesday as this system moves across the waters. There is a 60-90+% chance for gales north of Cape Falcon where a Gale Warning remains in effect from late this morning through Wednesday afternoon. South of Cape Falcon, there's only a 10-40% chance of gale force gusts through this evening, so have not opted for a Gale Warning. This evening through Wednesday, chances of gales increase between Cape Falcon and Cascade Head to 40-70%, so have kept the Gale Watch in place for zones PZZ253 and PZZ273 from this evening through Wednesday. A building west swell will increase seas to 14-19 ft around 14 seconds today into Wednesday. A Hazardous Seas Warning is in effect south of Cape Falcon beginning 1 PM today through Wednesday afternoon.
A stronger frontal system will increase winds and seas on Friday. with a 40-60% chance for Storm Force winds on Friday and a 60-80% chance of 20+ ft seas on Saturday. -03

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: A moderate to high sneaker wave threat continues along the coast through this week as a westerly swell of 10-12 ft at 13-15 seconds increases to 14-16 ft midweek. This will result in waves running up significantly farther on a beach than normal, including over rocks and jetties. Sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning.

There is also the potential for tidal overflow flooding Tuesday and Wednesday as the tide plus anomaly are forecasted between 10 and 11 ft (MLLW). This could lead to further water inundation and coastal erosion.

Additionally, confidence is increasing that a stronger westerly swell of 20-24 ft with a dominant period at 16-18 seconds will impact the coast on Saturday for dangerous surf conditions. Destructive waves may wash over beaches, jetties, and other structures unexpectedly.

Extreme caution should be used if you plan to visit beaches this week. The large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave. -03
